summary: A conceptual outline of an API for GRASP, to be used by Autonomic Service Agents when they call the GRASP module to exchange messages. Because GRASP is asynchronous, the API must be adapted to each programming environment.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8991 describes the set of function calls that a GRASP agent uses to talk to other agents. The agent says what it wants, such as find a peer, negotiate a value or publish one, and the GRASP core underneath deals with the messages, the timing and the caching. The RFC sets out the calls, the data they take and the values they return, without fixing any programming language.

questions: how do autonomic service agents use grasp
what is the grasp protocol api
subtitle: The programming interface an autonomic service agent uses to exchange messages with other agents.

tldr.problem: Autonomic service agents have to find peers, agree on values, and exchange state, and doing that directly in terms of protocol messages means every agent implements the protocol details itself.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an abstract application programming interface through which an agent registers itself and its objectives, discovers peers, negotiates, synchronizes and floods, with the GRASP core handling the protocol underneath.
tldr.outcome: The document is a conceptual outline rather than a formal specification, so language bindings and the exact details are left to implementations, and it leaves authorization of agents to particular objectives for future study.

today: RFC 8991 is an Informational document from May 2021 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It is a conceptual outline rather than a language-specific specification, so the binding details are left to the implementations, and the authorization of agents to particular objectives is left for future study.

sections.title: What the API Is For
sections.content:
An Autonomic Service Agent (ASA) is the atomic entity of an autonomic function, instantiated on autonomic nodes, and those nodes are members of a secure Autonomic Control Plane (ACP). When agents communicate with each other they should use the GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol (GRASP). GRASP relies on the message confidentiality and integrity provided by the ACP, so all nodes in a given Autonomic Network share the same trust boundary. Nodes that have not successfully joined the ACP cannot send, receive or intercept GRASP messages and cannot usurp ACP addresses. An ASA runs in an ACP node and therefore benefits from the node's security properties, and all agents within a given Autonomic Network therefore trust each other's messages. For these reasons, the API defined in the document has no explicit security features.

An important feature of GRASP is the concept of a GRASP objective, a data structure encoded like all GRASP messages in CBOR whose main contents are a name and a value. When an objective is passed from one agent to another, its value is either conveyed in one direction, by synchronization or flooding, or negotiated bilaterally. The semantics of the value are opaque to GRASP and therefore to the API, and each objective must be accurately specified in a dedicated specification that defines the syntax and semantics of the value, whether and how it supports negotiation, whether it supports a dry-run mode, and any other details needed for interoperability. The use of CBOR, with CDDL as the data definition language, allows the value to be passed between agents regardless of the programming languages in use. Data storage and consistency during negotiation are the responsibility of the agents involved.

A GRASP implementation could contain several sub-layers. The bottom layer is the GRASP base protocol module, responsible only for sending and receiving GRASP messages and maintaining shared data structures. Above that is the basic API this document describes, and the upper layer contains extended API functions built on the GRASP basic protocol. Multiple agents in a single node share the same instance of GRASP, much as multiple applications share a single TCP/IP stack, and this is hidden from individual agents by the API.

It is desirable that agents be portable user-space programs using a system-independent API, so in many implementations the GRASP code is split between user space and kernel space: in user space, library functions provide the API and communicate directly with the agents, and in kernel space a daemon, or a set of sub-services, provides the GRASP core functions that are independent of specific agents, such as multicast handling and relaying, and common data structures such as the discovery cache. The library and the core would communicate through an interprocess communication or system call mechanism, the details of which are system-dependent.

The functions provided by the API do not map one-to-one onto GRASP messages. They are intended to offer convenient support for message sequences, such as a discovery request followed by responses from several peers or a negotiation request followed by various possible responses, so that agent programmers can write code based on their application requirements rather than needing to understand protocol details. The document gives a conceptual outline of the API and is not a formal specification for any particular programming language or operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: An agent is a small program that does one job, and a whole set of them shares a network that is supposed to look after itself. GRASP is the protocol they use to find each other and agree on things. This RFC is the interface between an agent and that protocol, so an agent programmer writes calls like discover and negotiate rather than building and parsing messages.

sections.title: Asynchronous Operations and Overlapping Sessions
sections.content:
GRASP depends on asynchronous operations and wait states, and some of its messages are not idempotent, meaning that repeating a message may cause repeated changes of state in the recipient agent. Many agents will need to support several concurrent operations: an agent might need to negotiate one objective with a peer while discovering and synchronizing a different objective with a different peer, or an agent acting as a resource manager might need to run simultaneous negotiations for a given objective with several peers. Such an agent will probably need to support uninterruptible atomic changes to its internal data structures, using a mechanism provided by the operating system and programming language in use.

Three techniques are considered. In multithreading, the operating system and language provide the support for asynchronous operations, including thread creation, context switching, queues, locks and implicit wait states, so API calls can be treated as simple synchronous function calls within their own thread, even where the function includes wait states, blocking and queueing. Concurrent operations each run in their own thread: the discover() call may not return until discovery results have arrived or a timeout has occurred, so if the agent has other work to do, the call must be in a thread of its own. In an event loop with polling, blocking calls are not acceptable, so all calls must be non-blocking, and the main loop supports multiple GRASP sessions in parallel by repeatedly polling each for a change of state. The API implementation provides non-blocking versions of the functions that would otherwise block, and each call returns a noReply code instead of blocking until the event it is waiting for, or a failure, has occurred. The discover() call would return noReply instead of waiting, and would be repeated in every cycle of the main loop until it completes, effectively becoming a polling call. This does not repeat a message, so the fact that some GRASP messages are not idempotent, in particular each step in a negotiation session, is not a problem. In an event loop with callbacks, the agent programmer provides a callback function for each asynchronous operation, called asynchronously when a reply is received or a failure such as a timeout occurs.

GRASP allows an agent acting as a resource allocator for an objective to run two simultaneous negotiations with the same peer for different quantities of the resource, and the allocator must conduct two separate negotiation sessions at the same time with the same peer without mixing them up. Agents could be designed to avoid this, restricting themselves to one negotiation session at a time for a given objective, but that would be a voluntary restriction not required by the protocol, and GRASP assumes that any agent managing a resource may need multiple parallel negotiations, possibly with the same peer.

In the callback model, each agent therefore has to distinguish the sessions, and the peer's IP address is not sufficient. It is also not safe to rely on transport port numbers, since future variants of GRASP might use shared ports rather than a separate port per session. GRASP therefore includes a Session ID, and the API uses a session handle to distinguish simultaneous sessions, so that any number of sessions may proceed asynchronously in parallel. A GRASP session consists of a finite sequence of messages, for discovery, synchronization or negotiation, between two agents, and is uniquely identified on the wire by a pseudorandom Session ID plus the IP address of the initiator. On the first call in a new session the API returns a session_handle that identifies the session within the API, and a likely implementation forms the handle from the underlying GRASP Session ID and IP address. The handle must be used in all subsequent calls for the same session, and the GRASP core must keep state for each operation in progress, most likely keyed by the GRASP Session ID and the source address of the session initiator.

Sessions may terminate for numerous reasons: discovery succeeds or times out, negotiation succeeds or fails, a synchronization result is delivered, the other end fails to respond before a timeout, a loop count expires, or a network socket error occurs. A timeout at one end may result in a timeout or a socket error at the other end, since GRASP does not send error messages in this case. In all cases the API returns an appropriate code to the caller, which should then release any reserved resources, and after failure cases the GRASP specification recommends an exponential backoff before retrying.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in this protocol is instant, so the interface has to cope with waiting, and the RFC lays out three ways: one thread per operation, a polling loop that checks each session for progress, or callbacks that fire when something happens. Because one agent may run two negotiations with the same peer at once, each session gets its own handle, since the peer's address and port are not enough to tell them apart.

sections.title: The Shared Data Structures
sections.content:
Integers in the API are assumed to be 32-bit unsigned integers unless otherwise indicated. All functions return an unsigned errorcode as their first return value, where zero indicates success and any other value indicates failure of some kind. Three errorcodes have special importance: 1, Declined, meaning the other end has sent a Negotiation End message with a Decline option; 2, No reply, used in non-blocking calls to indicate that the other end has sent no reply so far; and 3, Unspecified error, used when no more specific error code applies. Appendix A gives a full list of currently suggested error codes, and while there is no absolute requirement for all implementations to use the same codes, this is highly recommended for portability of applications.

Whenever a timeout parameter appears it is an unsigned integer in milliseconds. If it is zero, the GRASP default timeout applies, with the exception of the discover() function, which has a different interpretation of a zero timeout. If no response is received before the timeout expires, the call fails unless otherwise noted.

An objective has a name as a UTF-8 string, three Boolean flags, a loop count and a value. The neg flag is true if the objective supports negotiation, synch if it supports synchronization, and dry if it supports dry-run negotiation, each defaulting to false. Only one of synch or neg may be true, and dry must not be true unless neg is also true. In some programming languages the preferred implementation may be to represent the flags as bits in a single byte, which is how they are encoded in GRASP messages; in others an enumeration might be preferable. The loop_count is an unsigned 8-bit integer limiting negotiation steps and defaulting to the GRASP default; the initiator of a negotiation sets it to a suitable value to prevent indefinite loops, and it is also used to limit the propagation of discovery and flood messages. The value is a data structure whose format is language dependent, with the constraint that it can be validly represented in CBOR. An important advantage of CBOR is that the value can be completely opaque to the GRASP core yet pass transparently through it, so the core can validate the syntax of a message but cannot validate the value of an objective, and it is the responsibility of each agent to validate the value it receives. Regardless of what other options exist for a language-specific representation, there must always be an option to use a raw CBOR data item as the value; the API wraps it with CBOR Tag 24 for transmission and unwraps it after reception, so agents can communicate regardless of programming language. The name and value fields are of variable length, and GRASP sets no maximum length for them, only for the total length of a GRASP message, though implementations might impose limits.

An asa_locator holds the actual locator, either an IP address or an ASCII string; the interface identifier index through which it was discovered; and the time on the local system clock when it will expire from the cache. The locator may be an IP address, a fully qualified domain name or a URI, these options being mutually exclusive, and it also records whether the locator was discovered via a Divert option, the applicable transport protocol and the applicable port number.

An asa_handle is provided as a very simple hook for an authentication and authorization scheme, which has not been defined. When an agent starts up it registers itself with the GRASP core, which returns an opaque handle that, although not cryptographically protected, would be difficult for a third party to predict, and the agent must present this handle in future calls. This prevents some elementary errors or trivial attacks, such as an agent manipulating an objective it has not registered to use. It is an up to 32-bit opaque value, only required to be unique within the local GRASP instance, valid until the agent terminates, and it should be unpredictable. A session_handle is likewise opaque to the agent and identifies calls to the API as belonging to a specific session; as well as distinguishing calls from different sessions, it allows GRASP to detect and ignore calls from non-existent or timed-out sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Most calls take the same handful of structures. An objective is a name, three flags saying what it can be used for, a step limit and an opaque value the protocol carries without understanding. A locator says where a peer is and when the entry goes stale. Two handles complete the picture: one proves the agent registered, and one names the session a call belongs to.

sections.title: The Function Groups and the Negotiation Sequence
sections.content:
The functions fall into several groups. Registration lets an agent register itself with the GRASP core and register the objectives it will manipulate. Discovery lets an agent that needs to initiate negotiation or synchronization of an objective find a peer willing to respond. Negotiation lets an agent act as initiator or responder for a negotiation session; after initiation negotiation is symmetric, so most of the functions can be used by either party. Synchronization lets an agent act as initiator or as responder and data source for a synchronization session. Flooding lets an agent send and receive an objective flooded to all nodes of the ACP. There is also a function for reporting an invalid message.

In the registration group, all agents must call register_asa() before any other API call, and it returns the asa_handle the agent must present in all subsequent calls. deregister_asa() removes all state for the agent and deregisters any objectives it registered, and the same must happen automatically if an agent exits. register_objective() must be used for any objective whose value the agent needs to transmit by negotiation, synchronization or flooding, but not for an objective it only wants to receive, and it takes a ttl giving the valid lifetime in milliseconds of any discovery response generated for the objective. A discoverable flag makes the objective immediately discoverable, for objectives defined only for discovery; an overlap flag allows more than one agent to register the same objective in the same GRASP instance, which is of value for the life cycle management of agents and must be used consistently for a given objective; and a local flag requires discovery to return a link-local address, for objectives that must be restricted to the local link.

The discover() function returns a list of discovered locators for a given objective, where an empty list means none were found within the timeout, which is not an error: GRASP discovery is not a deterministic process, and if several nodes handle an objective, none, some or all of them may be discovered before the timeout expires. The minimum_TTL parameter must be at least zero, and locally cached locators whose remaining time to live is less than or equal to it are deleted first, so a value of zero flushes all entries without affecting sessions already in progress. A timeout of zero returns the remaining cached locators immediately and takes no other action, so a call with both parameters zero is pointless.

Because the negotiation mechanism differs from a typical client or server exchange, the RFC illustrates the sequence of calls and GRASP messages. After the first protocol exchange the process is symmetrical, with the negotiating steps strictly alternating between the two sides, either side can end the negotiation, and the side due to respond next can insert a delay at any time to extend the other side's timeout, for example if an agent needed to negotiate with a third party first. The loop count embedded in the objective is initialized by the agent that starts a negotiation and is decremented by the GRASP core at each step before sending each M_NEGOTIATE message; if it reaches zero the negotiation fails and each side receives an error code. As the negotiation proceeds, each side updates the value of the objective according to its own semantics, though many objectives will have orderable values so that negotiation can be a simple bidding process, but that is not a requirement. Failure to agree, a timeout, or loop count exhaustion may all end a session, and none of these is a protocol failure.

The request_negotiate() function opens a negotiation session between two agents, and GRASP currently does not support multiparty negotiation. The peer parameter is the target node, and if it is null GRASP discovery is performed first to find a suitable peer. If the return code is zero there are two cases: the session handle may be null, in which case the negotiation succeeded in one exchange and the peer accepted the request, so the returned proffered objective holds the accepted value and no handle is needed; or the handle is not null, in which case the negotiation must continue, the returned proffered objective is the peer's first counter-offer and its contents must be used to prepare the next step, because it carries the updated loop count. The function must be followed by calls to negotiate_step, negotiate_wait or end_negotiate until the negotiation ends. A dry-run mode may or may not apply to a given session, but the two modes must not be mixed in one session.

The synchronize() function requests the synchronized value of an objective, and if the peer parameter is null and the objective is already in the local cache the flooded objective is returned immediately, ignoring the timeout. listen_synchronize() and stop_listen_synchronize() start and stop acting as a synchronization responder, and the former is non-blocking and may be repeated whenever the value changes. The flood() function floods one or more objectives and their values to all GRASP nodes, with a ttl giving the valid lifetime in milliseconds of the flooded data, where zero means infinity, and the locator tagging each objective is normally null but may be a valid locator for infrastructure agents that need to flood an address, protocol and port triplet. Each GRASP node caches the flooded objectives it receives until their time to live expires, and cached objectives are tagged with their origin as well as an expiry time, so multiple copies of the same objective may be cached at once. get_flood() returns the current value of a flooded objective, with the tagging locator letting the recipient tell copies from different sources apart, and expire_flood() lets an agent expire specific entries in the local flood cache when it decides a flooded value is stale.
sections.plainLanguage: The calls come in five groups: register yourself and your objectives, find a peer, negotiate with one, synchronise a value with one, and publish a value to everyone. Negotiation is the interesting one, because it is not a request and a reply: the two sides alternate proposals, either can walk away, and a step limit in the objective stops the exchange going round in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations for the GRASP protocol are discussed in the protocol specification itself. These include denial-of-service issues, even though these are considered a low risk in the ACP. In various places GRASP recommends an exponential backoff, and an agent using the API should use exponential backoff after failed discover, request_negotiate or synchronize operations, with the timescale depending on the semantics of the objective concerned. A flood operation should not be repeated at shorter intervals than is useful. These precautions are intended to assist the detection of denial-of-service attacks.

As a general precaution, all agents able to handle multiple negotiation or synchronization requests in parallel may protect themselves by limiting the number of requests they handle simultaneously and silently discarding excess requests. It might also be useful for the GRASP core to limit the number of objectives registered by a given agent, the total number of agents registered, and the total number of simultaneous sessions, to protect system resources. During times of high autonomic activity, such as recovery from widespread faults, agents may experience many session failures.

The trust model is that all agents in a given Autonomic Network communicate via a secure autonomic control plane and therefore trust each other's messages. Specific authorization of agents to use particular GRASP objectives is a subject for future study. A malicious agent could extend a negotiation session indefinitely by use of the negotiate_wait function or by manipulating the loop count of an objective, and a robustly implemented agent could detect such behaviour by a peer and break off the negotiation.

The asa_handle is the first line of defence against a malware process attempting to imitate a legitimately registered agent, and the session_handle is the first line of defence against one attempting to hijack a GRASP session. Both are likely to be created using GRASP's 32-bit pseudorandom Session ID, and by construction GRASP avoids the risk of Session ID collisions. There remains a finite probability that an attacker could guess a Session ID, session handle or asa_handle, but this would only be of value to an attacker that had already penetrated the ACP, which would allow many other simpler forms of attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the network is assumed to be secure already, the API has no security features of its own, and the RFC is mostly about not being a nuisance. Failed calls should be retried with a growing delay, floods should not be repeated too often, and an agent that can handle many requests at once should set a limit and drop the excess, so that a misbehaving peer cannot take the node down.

messages.label: M_NEGOTIATE
messages.note: negotiate_step() answers with a counter-offer. The steps alternate strictly between the two sides.

messages.label: M_NEGOTIATE
messages.note: The counter-offer carries the updated loop count.

messages.label: M_WAIT
messages.note: negotiate_wait() inserts a delay, extending the other side's timeout.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS TO HANDLE ASYNCHRONOUS OPERATIONS

items.title: Multithreading
items.text: Each operation gets its own thread, and the API calls can block inside it. The agent must put a long call such as discover() in a thread of its own.

items.title: Event loop with polling
items.text: All calls are non-blocking and return a noReply code, and the main loop repeats them each cycle until they complete. No message is ever sent twice this way.

items.title: Event loop with callbacks
items.text: The agent supplies a callback for each operation, and GRASP calls it asynchronously when a reply arrives or a failure such as a timeout occurs.

viz.caption: THE ERROR CODES WITH SPECIAL MEANING

items.label: Declined
items.desc: The other end sent a Negotiation End message with a Decline option.

items.label: No reply
items.desc: In a non-blocking call, the other end has sent no reply so far.

items.label: Unspecified error
items.desc: Used when no more specific error code applies.
